content:
A new open source tool is going viral online because it promises to give users who have no interest in Apple Intelligence back 12GB or more of storage on their Mac. Here are the details.

"Turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and remove downloaded models"

Like many companies adding AI tools and models to their platforms, Apple has faced criticism for features some users deem unnecessary taking up storage space.

Apple Intelligence required up to 7GB of storage during the macOS 26 era, but that figure has grown significantly with macOS 27, where Apple now says its newest models can require up to 14GB on the latest Macs.

In response, independent developer Om Lahore released a project called RemoveMacAI on GitHub late last week, claiming it can "turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and remove downloaded models".

Lahore explained that his tool applies a configuration profile, using Apple's own restriction keys to disable Apple Intelligence, while also leveraging the company's asset service to remove downloaded models and prevent macOS from downloading them again.

He also detailed in full what the tool removes, which features it disables, and what users can expect after running it:

Disabled features: Siri (including "Hey Siri" and the menu bar icon), Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, ChatGPT extensions, summaries in Mail, Messages, Safari, Notes, and notifications, Mail smart replies, inline text predictions, Spatial Photos, the Photos Clean Up tool, and Xcode predictive code completion. Removed models: Apple Intelligence foundation models, as well as models used for image generation and Genmoji, Spatial Photos, the Photos Clean Up tool, and Xcode code completion.

and

Lahore pointed out that dictation will still be usable after running RemoveMacAI, as it "is a separate setting, and its language models were not removed."

He finally added that the entire process is reversible, with full details and instructions available here.

9to5Mac's take

Although some of the strong pushback against how much storage Apple Intelligence takes up on Mac seems to match the reflexive aversion to anything AI-related, reclaiming 12GB or more is a legitimate argument for users with limited built-in storage—especially those with just 256GB Macs.

The more fundamental question is one of basic control over your own operating system: users who have zero interest in Apple Intelligence should have a straightforward way to fully disable it and reclaim the storage its models occupy, just as they can with other applications and optional system components.

That said, it's impossible to predict whether Apple will try to have the project taken down from GitHub, or change macOS's underlying mechanisms to make Apple Intelligence models harder to remove.

Likewise, there's no way to know what long-term effects disabling or removing these components might have on macOS itself, or even on third-party applications that increasingly rely on Apple's models to deliver basic functionality.

Although RemoveMacAI is open source and does not require disabling System Integrity Protection, it still relies on configuration profiles, restriction keys, and system services—things Apple can change at any time.

That means future macOS updates could partially break the tool, or cause users to run into unexpected behaviour before the project is updated.

For now, anyone considering using RemoveMacAI should understand this is an unofficial third-party tool that makes system-level changes, and should be comfortable with how it operates.

To be very clear, RemoveMacAI appears to be a well-intentioned open source project aimed at giving Mac users more autonomy and control over what runs on their machine and how its storage is used. It's just impossible to know whether Apple will see it the same way.
